  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1111,
      "endEvent": 1114,
      "contextStartEvent": 1097,
      "contextEndEvent": 1183,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "why shouldn't we presume he has reasons for all of them",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The move from reasons for some evils to reasons for all could shelter unexplained suffering without establishing the generalization. However, Horn supplies proposed reasons and analogies at E1115–E1183, including qualified animal compensation. This is an ordinary inductive argument; whether its presumption excludes contrary evidence regardless of merits remains unclear."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2413,
      "endEvent": 2424,
      "contextStartEvent": 2374,
      "contextEndEvent": 2427,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "any negative experience we have in this life",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Infinite future happiness is proposed as compensation for any earthly negative experience, potentially making every suffering pattern compatible with divine love. But Horn expressly denies that this licenses arbitrary treatment at E2421–E2424 and retains the need for good reasons at E2425–E2427. The protective scope is therefore uncertain, not unrestricted."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2466,
      "endEvent": 2469,
      "contextStartEvent": 2462,
      "contextEndEvent": 2536,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "just because i can't see a good reason doesn't mean that it's it's not there",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The repeatable maxim challenges an inference from unseen reasons to absent reasons. Horn supports that limited distinction with a painting analogy and proposes particular goods at E2497–E2536. His claim that their existence need not be proved could protect the argument, but the ongoing target is also Watkins's explicitly logical impossibility claim."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2997,
      "endEvent": 3009,
      "contextStartEvent": 2964,
      "contextEndEvent": 3009,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "god can always bring a greater good from any evil that exists",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Horn expressly says evidential objections evaporate given his proofs, then requires atheists to show that justifying reasons are impossible. This neutralizes contrary suffering through unrestricted possible goods rather than establishing their actual likelihood. The qualification is substantial: he conditions this on independent arguments for God and acknowledges free will does not explain every case."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 3182,
      "endEvent": 3193,
      "contextStartEvent": 3157,
      "contextEndEvent": 3214,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "then there must be some reason he does not make his existence obvious",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Asked whether reasonable unbelief decreases God's probability, Horn makes unexplained hiddenness require an unseen reason once his proofs are accepted, adding compensation and unknown goods at E3191–E3214. This protects against the proposed contrary pattern. It remains conditional on independent proofs, and E3157–E3168 explicitly avoids branding unbelievers unreasonable people."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 3578,
      "endEvent": 3587,
      "contextStartEvent": 3553,
      "contextEndEvent": 3590,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "is incapable of having reasons to justify that",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "In renewed closing use, Horn rejects the evidential case because Watkins did not establish God's incapacity to possess justifying reasons. Requiring impossibility shields possible unseen purposes from likelihood-based objections. Horn explicitly grounds this move in his earlier positive arguments at E3583–E3585; it is a protected argument, not an unsupported catchphrase."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 3774,
      "endEvent": 3776,
      "contextStartEvent": 3756,
      "contextEndEvent": 3783,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "we all have nothing to lose and everything to gain from an honest pursuit of truth",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The absolute reassurance supplies a reason to pursue truth without establishing that such pursuit carries no losses, immediately after acknowledging unwelcome implications at E3762–E3769. However, it may express an overriding epistemic value rather than deny practical costs. That ambiguity prevents confirming substitution; nothing here immunizes beliefs against criticism."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 2923,
      "endEvent": 2944,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the existence of mere causation could probably go either way between naturalism and theism",
      "explanation": "Horn grants that causation alone does not favor his position, then distinguishes specific causal features he thinks do. This limits the conclusion and connects it to his previously developed arguments."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2697,
      "endEvent": 2722,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "if i were to have a cogent religious experience",
      "explanation": "Watkins acknowledges evidence favoring theism and identifies an experience that could outweigh his argument from evil. This explicitly leaves his conclusion open to contrary evidence, while requiring the experience to be cogent."
    }
